clinicalPearls: The hallmark sign is corneal guttae, focal excrescences of Descemet membrane that give the endothelium a beaten-metal appearance on slit-lamp retroillumination.
The corneal endothelium is a non-regenerating monolayer; progressive cell loss causes failure of the deturgescence pump with resulting stromal and epithelial oedema.
A classic symptom is blurred vision that is worst on waking and improves through the day as surface evaporation clears overnight oedema.
The disease is typically bilateral but asymmetric, shows a female predominance and usually becomes symptomatic in later decades.
A trinucleotide repeat expansion in the TCF4 gene is the strongest known genetic association, while COL8A2 variants underlie rarer early-onset forms.
Advanced disease progresses to bullous keratopathy, with painful epithelial bullae and eventual subepithelial scarring and vascularisation.
Endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK or DSAEK) has largely replaced penetrating keratoplasty and offers faster, more reliable visual recovery.
Intraocular surgery, particularly cataract extraction, can precipitate endothelial decompensation, so endothelial status must be assessed and counselled beforehand.
reference.pathophysiology: The corneal endothelium is a terminally differentiated, essentially non-dividing monolayer that maintains corneal clarity by acting as both a barrier and an active metabolic pump, drawing fluid out of the stroma to keep it in a relatively dehydrated (deturgescent) state. In Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy, accelerated endothelial cell apoptosis, oxidative stress and abnormal extracellular matrix deposition produce guttae and a steady decline in endothelial cell density. The commonly implicated TCF4 trinucleotide repeat expansion is thought to generate toxic repeat-containing RNA that sequesters splicing regulators, an RNA-mediated mechanism analogous to that seen in myotonic dystrophy. Once endothelial density falls below a critical level the pump can no longer counter passive fluid influx; the stroma imbibes water and swells, oedema extends to the epithelium to form microcysts and bullae, and chronic decompensation leads to subepithelial fibrosis, scarring and vascularisation with progressive loss of vision.
additionalDifferentials: Corneal oedema from chronically raised intraocular pressure
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to identify guttae, corneal oedema and bullae
Specular microscopy for endothelial cell density, pleomorphism and polymegathism
Corneal pachymetry and thickness mapping to quantify oedema
Scheimpflug tomography, including posterior corneal changes
Genetic testing for TCF4 repeat expansion where indicated
redFlags: New ocular pain or foreign-body sensation suggesting ruptured epithelial bullae
Rapid corneal decompensation following intraocular surgery
An epithelial defect with infiltrate raising concern for microbial keratitis on bullous keratopathy
Sudden marked reduction in vision with dense corneal oedema
reference.prognosis: The condition is slowly progressive over years; with timely endothelial keratoplasty visual outcomes are generally good, though graft survival, rejection and the need for repeat surgery remain long-term considerations.
pitfalls: Failing to identify guttae and counsel or plan appropriately before cataract or refractive surgery, risking postoperative decompensation.
Attributing characteristic morning blurring to other causes and missing the diagnosis.
Relying on central pachymetry alone rather than assessing endothelial morphology and function.
Mistaking herpetic endotheliitis for primary dystrophic decompensation.
Underestimating the pain and functional impact of bullous keratopathy in advanced disease.
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course (standard reference)
management: Topical hypertonic sodium chloride drops and ointment to draw fluid from the oedematous stroma and clear morning blurring
Warm-air evaporation on waking as a simple measure to reduce overnight epithelial oedema
Bandage contact lens, ocular lubricants and analgesia for painful epithelial bullae in bullous keratopathy
Endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK or DSAEK) as definitive treatment for visually significant corneal decompensation, with penetrating keratoplasty reserved for advanced scarring
Endothelial-protective cataract surgery, staged or combined with keratoplasty where the cornea is borderline
Monitor endothelial cell density and corneal thickness with specular microscopy and pachymetry
Long-term surveillance for graft rejection and failure after keratoplasty, with prophylactic topical corticosteroids
